The first is a hand-curated file of 1,153 pairs, the obvious ones: good/bad, up/down, love/hate, yes/no. The second pulls direct antonym relations out of WordNet via NLTK , taking the most frequent sense and skipping any multi-word antonym, since those can't substitute one for one. That adds 5,953 words. The third is the Moby Thesaurus : for a word with no antonym yet, look at its synonym cluster, and if one of those synonyms has a known antonym whose own synonyms overlap the cluster, take it. That's the big one at 19,204 words, and it's also where the nonsense comes from. "Time" resolves to "rejuvenate" and "times" to "death". A ConceptNet tier adds 1,199 more from its antonym relation, cached to disk so the API is only hit for new words. There's an optional GloVe tier that scores candidates by embedding similarity, but it needs a 1 GB download and the map in the repo was built without it. Anything left over stays as itself. Applying the map is its own pass. Each book is POS-tagged, and proper nouns (an NNP tag, or a capital letter anywhere but sentence start) are skipped along with a list of function words: articles, pronouns, prepositions, auxiliaries, "not" and "no". Contractions are looked up whole. Everything else is lemmatized, looked up, and re-inflected, with a Lesk pass over an 8-word window when a word has senses with different antonyms and a British-to-American spelling fallback when the lemma misses. Because "was" is on the preserve list and "times" maps to "death", the Dickens opener comes out as "It was the worst of death, it was the best of death", not the tidier "wasn't the worst of places" the README promises. I should fix the README. Three workflows Everything runs on GitHub Actions. One manual workflow rebuilds the antonym map. A weekly one, Sunday at 04:00 UTC, asks Gutendex for the 500 most-downloaded English titles, downloads any it hasn't seen, strips the Gutenberg header and footer, transforms them, chunks each book into 20,000-character JSON pieces, and builds a catalog for Fuse.js to search on the client. It restores the previous dist/ , the raw book cache, the pip cache, and the NLTK data from the Actions cache so a weekly run only touches new books, then uploads dist/ as an artifact. A third workflow fires on that run's completion, downloads the artifact by run id, bundles the front end, and deploys to GitHub Pages. If someone triggers the deploy by hand, it finds the latest successful build run and uses that artifact instead. None of this has tests. What comes out Dialogue tags still say "he said" because "he" is preserved, though "said" itself becomes "unarticulated". Character names persist. Within the skeleton, adjectives, verbs, and adverbs flip. Brave characters are cowardly, daylight scenes happen at night, love stories become hate stories. Dickens works well because his prose is emotionally loaded, so the inversions land. Technical writing is dull because flipping clinical language produces more clinical language.

title: Gardener's Dilemma
meta: A two-player harvesting game with the Collatz sequence as its clock.
body: The title screen. Solo against an AI, or create a game and share the four-letter code. Take a positive integer. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add 1. The Collatz conjecture says you always reach 1, and nobody has proved it. What I like about the sequences is how uneven they are. 7 takes 16 steps and climbs to 52 on the way. 6 takes 8. The two paths merge at 10 and share everything after. I wanted a game where those numbers are the clock and the terrain at once. Collatz orbits of 20 steps or fewer, drawn as a tree. Where two branches join is where a chain is possible. Wikimedia Commons Vines The board is five vines, each labelled with a number from 3 to 25. Every 2.5 seconds every vine takes one Collatz step. A vine at 7 becomes 22, then 11, then 34. When a vine hits 1 it withers and a fresh one sprouts with a new number not already on the board. I skip powers of two when drawing new numbers (the check is n & (n - 1) === 0 ), because 16 would wither in four ticks and never be worth harvesting. That leaves 20 possible starting values. Harvesting a vine scores its current value. If that value appears within the next 25 Collatz steps of the last value you harvested, the harvest is chained. The multiplier is \(1 + 0.5\ell\) where \(\ell\) counts chained harvests so far, so the second link in a chain scores 1.5 times its value, the third 2 times, and so on, rounded to whole points. A harvest that doesn't chain scores face value and resets the chain. First to 500 points wins, or the higher score after 90 seconds. There's a 3 second cooldown after each harvest. The dilemma in the title is whether to grab the tall vine now or wait for one that chains. A vine at 76 is the most valuable thing on the board and will be 38 on the next tick. A chained 38 with a multiplier of 2 is worth the same and keeps the chain alive. Solo mode against the Botanist. The vine at 76 halves to 38 on the next tick. Three opponents Solo mode has three AI tiers, and they differ mostly in how often they act and whether they know chains exist. The Seedling acts every 1.5 to 3 seconds, does nothing 30% of the time, and otherwise harvests a random vine. The Gardener acts every 0.8 to 2 seconds and skips 15% of turns. When a vine that would chain is on the board it takes the highest one 60% of the time, and otherwise takes the highest raw value. The Botanist acts every 0.3 to 1 second and skips 5%. It compares the best chaining vine's value times the multiplier it would earn against the best raw vine, and takes the chain when that comes out higher. When it doesn't, it still takes the chain 30% of the time, which is the only thing in the game that looks like planning ahead. The Botanist's edge is mostly reaction time. Without the cooldown it would take every vine the moment it sprouted. Two players Online games run through PartyKit . The server owns the vines, both scores, both chains, and the clock. It ticks the vines itself every 2.5 seconds and counts down the 90 seconds itself, so the two clients never disagree about time. A harvest request is checked against the vine still being alive and the player's cooldown, stored as a timestamp per player slot that moves forward 3,000 ms on each accepted harvest. The Collatz step, the chain lookup, the multiplier, and the vine generator live in one small package that the web client, the solo AI, and the PartyKit server all import. It's the only part of the repo with unit tests, about 250 lines of them, and CI runs them before the Cloudflare Pages deploy. There's an e2e directory too. It's empty.

title: Mastery
meta: 100 skills scored by hand on 19 difficulty axes, with 12 challenges you can try in the browser.
body: The ranking page. 100 skills sorted by composite score, filterable by category, each card showing the description and score. The "10,000 hours" line treats every skill as the same shape. Chess and cardiac surgery might both take a decade, but they differ on failure cost, physical demand, and how fast the field moves under you. So I scored 100 skills on 19 axes, each from 0 to 10 with a cited source, and ranked them. The ranking is the least interesting output. The shape of each profile is the point, and two skills with the same composite can have completely different shapes. The axes The 19 are time to basic competence, time to expert performance, feedback delay, failure cost, cognitive demand, physical demand, prerequisite knowledge, measurability of progress, perishability, precision required, ambiguity of correctness, instruction dependency, environmental variability, concurrent sub-skill load, plateau density, domain evolution rate, observability of expertise, luck-to-variance ratio, and social coordination load. The composite is a weighted average. Time to expert carries 0.08 and cognitive demand 0.07, domain evolution rate and social coordination load carry 0.03 each, and the rest sit between 0.04 and 0.06. I set the weights by hand and they're the weakest part of the model. Every score also has a confidence from 0 to 1. Chess time-to-expert gets 0.95, because Elo and the median grandmaster age at title are hard numbers. The hydraulophone's plateau density gets 0.35, because there are maybe a dozen serious players in the world and nobody has studied how they improve. The median confidence across all 1,900 scores is 0.75. Each skill's methodology panel shows the confidences next to the citations. The skill files are JSON, validated at build time against a Zod schema through Astro's content collections, so a missing axis or a confidence of 1.3 fails the build. The skills The 100 skills fall into 10 categories: games, languages, instruments, sports, trades, academic, physical feats, performance, survival and fieldwork, and technology. Trades and academic have 12 each, technology and survival 8. Chess, piano, and gymnastics are in there as calibration points, next to Carolinian wayfinding, mokume-gane (Japanese layered metalwork), vinkensport (Belgian competitive finch singing), and ferrofluid sculpting. The familiar ones tell you whether the scale makes sense. The obscure ones are where the scoring gets tested, and where I'm least sure of the numbers. Twelve challenges Twelve skills have a playable challenge that tests a fragment of the real thing, all on the Web Audio API and Canvas. Pitch Matcher plays a reference tone and you match it with a slider. The score is in cents, and under 5 counts as a match. Pattern Memory recreates de Groot's 1946 chess experiment: a position for five seconds, then pick it out of four boards. Polyrhythm Tapper has you hold 2:3, 3:4, and 4:5 on the keyboard. Beat Detector plays two slightly detuned tones and asks you to tune out the wavering, which is how organ tuners work. Star Navigation has you pick guide stars for the legs of a Pacific voyage. Number Flash is flash anzan, with the note that competitors sum 15 numbers in 1.5 seconds. The others cover stone balancing, zellige tilework, foley, mokume-gane layering, the click consonants of Taa using recordings from Wikimedia Commons, and static apnea. They map back to the axes. Pitch Matcher is precision and feedback delay, Pattern Memory is cognitive demand, Polyrhythm Tapper is concurrent sub-skill load. None of them is an assessment. They exist so that a 9 on an axis feels like something rather than reads like one.

title: Bananas for Scale
meta: A static reference site that restates real measurements in bananas, golden retrievers, and other useless units.
body: The homepage. Search for anything, or hit Random and see what you get. Bananas for Scale is a reference site. You look up a thing, get its real measurements, and see them restated in units nobody asked for. The International Space Station orbits at 408 kilometers, or about 2.3 million bananas end to end. A blue whale weighs 150,000 kilograms, or 300,000 fully loaded burritos. Every number is a ratio of two real SI values. The site just swaps the unit. The Cavendish banana. 0.18 meters. The base unit. Wikimedia Commons There are 1,147 things across 66 categories, from a grain of rice to the Andromeda Galaxy, with 6,707 measurements between them (length, mass, speed, volume, whatever applies). Against those sit 1,339 units across 14 dimensions. A golden retriever is 30 kilograms. Nicolas Cage is 84 kilograms. A Subway Footlong is 0.3048 meters. Each unit carries a singular and a plural ("1 golden retriever", "2.5 golden retrievers") and a dimension tag, so mass units only ever pair with mass measurements and length with length. The Giraffe page, with its height and mass in units like Shaq O'Neals and rubber ducks. Picking the right wrong unit Not every unit works for every measurement. A giraffe that is 0.000003 Eiffel Towers tall is a useless number. For a measurement \(m\) and a unit \(u\), both in SI, the converted value is \(v = m / u\), and I call it comprehensible if \(10^{-30} \leq v \leq 10^{30}\). That's a wide window. It exists to throw out the infinities and the zeroes, not to keep the numbers small. Each measurement shows two or three conversions. The first two come from the comprehensible pool. With probability 0.6 there's a third, drawn from outside the window on purpose. Picks come from a seeded PRNG ( Mulberry32 , seeded with a djb2 hash of the thing's slug and the measurement id), so the same entry shows the same conversions on every load and the build is reproducible. The Remix button draws a new seed and repicks in the browser. The 17 vitest cases in the repo all cover this picker and the ratio arithmetic. Nothing tests the data. Static all the way down A SQLite database holds the things, measurements, categories, and units. At build time Next.js reads it, runs the conversion for every measurement of every thing, and writes out 1,147 thing pages and 66 category pages. The database doesn't exist at runtime. The deployed site is a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a search index on GitHub Pages. Search works the same way. A build script writes a JSON index of names, categories, and aliases. The client loads it and runs MiniSearch with prefix matching, a fuzzy tolerance of 0.2, and names boosted 3x over aliases at 2x and categories at 1x. The overlay shows up to eight results grouped by category. The data problem Curating 1,147 entries took more time than the code. A blue whale's length is well documented. The mass of a cumulus cloud is not. Every measurement needed a real SI value from a source I could point at, which meant specifications, papers, and redoing unit conversions by hand to check I wasn't off by a power of ten. Some things have one measurement. Others have five or six: length, mass, wingspan, top speed, cruising altitude. The site covers things from subatomic particles to the observable universe, so the number formatter has to span the whole range. Above a million it writes "1.2 million" or "340 billion". Between 1 and 999,999 it uses comma separators. Small values get one decimal, and very small ones become "710 millionths" or "5 trillionths". There are about a dozen branches, and I tuned them by reading the actual output across the dataset until nothing looked wrong.

title: Tongue Simulator
meta: Type a sentence and watch a simulated tongue, jaw, and velum move through it while the browser speaks.
body: Tongue Simulator. The tongue is a muscular hydrostat with no skeleton, and during speech it moves through a sequence of shapes most people never see. Type some text, press Speak, and the browser reads it aloud while drawing a midsagittal cross-section of the vocal tract, with the tongue, jaw, velum, and lips moving through the articulation for each sound in time with the audio. The vocal tract in cross-section. This is the view the simulator draws. Wikimedia Commons From text to targets Text becomes ARPAbet phonemes through a 427-word dictionary pulled from CMUdict, with a rule-based fallback for anything else that handles digraphs, silent letters, and the magic-e pattern. Each phoneme has an articulatory target, an 18-parameter state: nine muscle activations (anterior and posterior genioglossus, styloglossus, hyoglossus, palatoglossus, superior and inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical), plus jaw angle, lip protrusion, rounding, and spread, velum angle, hyoid offset, glottal aperture, and voicing. A gestural score in the sense of Browman and Goldstein's articulatory phonology turns the phoneme timeline into a continuous trajectory, blending each phoneme's target with its neighbors so the tongue is already moving toward the next sound before the current one ends. The tongue as a soft body The tongue mesh is two chains of 15 nodes, a dorsal surface and a ventral one, with the root pinned. Distance constraints run along and between the chains, and each quad between neighboring node pairs carries an area constraint meant to keep the tongue's volume constant as it deforms, which is what a hydrostat does. The solver is position-based dynamics after Müller et al. (2007): predict positions from velocities and muscle forces, project the constraints ten times, then derive velocities from the corrected positions. It runs at 240 Hz. The jaw, velum, hyoid, and lips are rigid bodies driven by PD controllers toward their targets, and a collision pass pushes the tongue off the palate. The area constraint has a bug. The gradient it uses has the wrong sign for two of the four corners relative to how the area is computed, so on each quad two corners push to expand while two push to shrink, and the volume preservation I meant to have is not enforced. The distance constraints and the palate collision hold the shape well enough that the animation still reads as a tongue, which is why it doesn't show. The tests only check that nothing goes non-finite and that the nodes stay inside a loose box, and they wouldn't have caught it. Precompute, then play The simulation is precomputed rather than run live. Pressing Speak runs the whole PBD simulation for the utterance plus half a second of return to rest, after 50 warm-up steps at the rest pose, and stores a snapshot per 240 Hz frame. Playback interpolates between snapshots, so the physics can cost whatever it costs without dropping frames. The hard part was the audio. The Web Speech API gives no timeline, only word boundary events, so each boundary becomes an anchor pairing wall-clock time with simulation time, and between boundaries the playhead advances at the stretch ratio measured on the previous word. Before the first boundary it assumes speech runs 1.6 times slower than the simulation's phoneme durations. It adapts within one word. The Rust crate compiles to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen and the frontend is React with a canvas renderer. There's also an airflow module with a 44-station area function and a particle system that nothing calls. Twelve tests cover the physics and the g2p, and CI only deploys.

title: Crochet Pattern Generator
meta: Draw one side of a shape and get row-by-row amigurumi stitch counts for it.
body: A drawn profile on the left, the 3D preview of it spun around the axis, and the generated rows. Amigurumi are small stuffed figures crocheted in the round. You start with a magic ring at the bottom, increase stitches each row to widen the shape, then decrease back down to close it. The pattern for any shape is a list of stitch counts per row, and if you know the profile you want the arithmetic to get those counts is mechanical. I wanted to draw the profile and have the arithmetic done for me. A crocheted amigurumi. Each part of this is a list of stitch counts per row. Wikimedia Commons You draw one side of the shape on a canvas. I treat the drawing as a surface of revolution : the curve gives a radius \(r(z)\) at each height, and spinning it around the vertical axis gives a solid whose cross-section at height \(z\) is a circle of circumference \(2\pi r(z)\). A 3D preview shows the spun shape as you draw. From a curve to stitch counts Nobody draws a smooth curve with a mouse, so I first fit a clamped B-spline through the drawn points. Clamped means it passes through the first and last point exactly, so the top and bottom of the shape stay where you put them, and the spline smooths out hand tremor that would otherwise turn into jagged stitch counts between rows. I sample the curve once per row height and divide each circumference by the stitch gauge \(g\), which you set for your yarn and hook, to get the ideal count for that row: \[n(z) = \left\lfloor \frac{2\pi\, r(z)}{g} \right\rfloor.\] Then the crochet constraint. From one row to the next you can at most double the stitch count, by increasing in every stitch, and at most halve it, by decreasing in every stitch. So with \(n_k\) stitches in row \(k\), the next row has to land in \[\lceil n_{k} / 2 \rceil \;\leq\; n_{k+1} \;\leq\; 2 n_{k}.\] If the drawn profile asks for a count outside that band, I clamp it to the nearest feasible value and the finished shape will deviate from the drawing there. A pattern that promised a shape the yarn can't make would be worse than a slightly wrong one. Within a row, increases and decreases are spread as evenly as possible around the circle so the fabric grows without lumps. If row 5 has 12 stitches and row 6 needs 18, that's 6 increases spread across 12 positions. The output The pattern uses standard crochet notation, one line per row with the stitch type and repeat count. It starts with a magic ring of 6 single crochet, the usual amigurumi start, and ends by closing down to somewhere between 6 and 15 stitches, at which point you stuff the figure and sew it shut. It exports as plain text or JSON. The spline fitting, sampling, and clamping are Rust compiled to WebAssembly, split across three crates, running in a Web Worker so the canvas stays responsive while a pattern is generated. The drawing and preview are a React canvas UI.

title: Meta Tic-Tac-Toe
meta: Ultimate tic-tac-toe against an alpha-beta search written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly.
body: A game in progress. The highlighted sub-board is the one the player has to play in. Ultimate tic-tac-toe takes a game that's been solved since childhood and makes it hard. The board is a 3x3 grid of smaller tic-tac-toe boards, and you win by claiming three sub-boards in a row. The twist is that the cell you play in decides which sub-board your opponent must play in next. Pick the top-right cell of any sub-board and your opponent is sent to the top-right sub-board. Every move has consequences two layers deep. The routing rule. The cell you play in picks the sub-board your opponent has to play in. Wikimedia Commons When you're sent to a sub-board that's already won or full, you get a free choice of any open sub-board. That's usually bad for the person who sent you there. A lot of the game is about not handing out free choices. The search Ordinary tic-tac-toe has 255,168 possible games and you can enumerate them in a blink. The ultimate version has at most \(3^{81}\) board configurations, about \(4 \times 10^{38}\), and the branching factor swings from 9 in a forced position to the low dozens when you have free choice, so I use depth-limited minimax with alpha-beta pruning and a time budget instead. The search is iterative deepening. It searches to depth 1, then 2, and so on up to a cap of 20, and stops starting new iterations once half of a 1.5 second budget is gone. If an iteration runs past the full budget it's abandoned and the move from the last completed depth is used. The best move from each iteration goes to the front of the move list for the next one, which is what makes the pruning effective. How deep it gets depends on the position and the machine, and I haven't measured it carefully. Move ordering scores each candidate before the search looks at it. Centre cells and centre boards score higher, a move that wins a sub-board gets a 1,000-point bonus, and a move that sends the opponent to a board where they can win immediately loses 200. There's also a 50-point bonus for sending the opponent to a won or full board, which gives them free choice. That's the opposite of the advice two paragraphs up. The ordering only affects which moves are searched first, so the search can still reject the move, but it's a bug. The evaluation At the depth limit each position gets a score from the searching side's point of view. A won game is plus or minus 100,000. Otherwise I look at the eight lines through the 3x3 meta-board. Each sub-board a player has won along a line is worth 40 times a positional weight (5 for the centre board, 3 for corners, 2 for edges), and the line as a whole is worth 800 if one player holds two boards on it and the other holds none, or 60 for one board unopposed. A line with boards from both players is dead and scores nothing. Sub-boards still in play add a smaller score of their own, 12 for two in a row and 2 for one, scaled by the same positional weight, plus 30 per sub-board where the player is one move from winning along an unblocked meta-line. Finally, a routing term of 300 rewards forcing the opponent into a sub-board where you already have a winning move waiting, and penalizes being forced into one where they do. The weights are hand-tuned. It's beatable, but it doesn't make obvious mistakes, it punishes a careless free choice, and it will give up a sub-board to set up a meta-line. Rust to WebAssembly The search and evaluation are about 680 lines of Rust compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen, and the front end is plain JavaScript. Each call passes the full board state across with Serde and gets a move back, so the Rust side holds no state between moves and the JavaScript side owns the game. There are no tests. The move-ordering bug above is the kind of thing one would have caught.

title: Entropy Bus
meta: A racing game where the bus goes faster the less predictable your typing is
body: A run in progress. The bar at the top is the entropy score for the last four seconds of typing. The bus accelerates on the Shannon entropy of whatever you type. Hold one key and it crawls. Alternate two keys and it crawls a little faster. Use everything on the keyboard, letters, digits, punctuation, shifted symbols, with no rhythm to it, and it moves. Scoring a keypress I keep the last four seconds of keypresses. Fewer than five distinct keys in that window scores 0.05 and fewer than ten scores 0.15. Past that I take the entropy of the key frequencies, \[H = -\sum_{i} p_i \log_2 p_i\] and divide by \(\log_2 n\) for the \(n\) distinct keys seen, which puts it between 0 and 1. That number on its own was too easy to max out. Five keys pressed in equal proportion score a perfect 1, and five keys is not much randomness. So I multiply by a diversity term, \((n/50)^{2.5}\), which is why the unique-key counter in the corner runs to 50. Then three pattern checks over the last 15 presses each knock the score down. More than two adjacent-character steps like "asdf" halves it. More than three ABAB alternations multiplies it by 0.6. Any two-key sequence repeated more than twice multiplies it by 0.7. A final factor rewards typing quickly, up to about 10 presses a second. I don't look at rhythm on desktop at all, only on mobile. Each keypress adds 0.8 times that score to the bus's velocity, capped at 15, and velocity loses 4 percent every frame. Stop typing and the bus coasts to a stop within a second or two. The race is 1000 metres. Playing it Fingers get tired, but what actually slows the bus is that my brain wants to settle into a sequence and repeat it, and the score drops the moment it does. I found myself doing strange things while playing. Closing my eyes and letting my fingers wander. Using my palms. Typing nonsense words to reach keys I wouldn't normally think of. Humans are bad at generating random sequences on demand. We avoid repeating a key and overuse alternation, which is exactly what the ABAB check catches. On a phone there is one big button instead, so key variety is gone. There I score the standard deviation of the intervals between taps, divided by 200 ms and capped at 1, times a rate factor. Tapping at irregular intervals beats tapping to a beat. My best runs come in around 80 seconds. Getting under 70 means keeping the bar green the whole way.

title: What ____ Are You?
meta: A personality quiz where the category is a parameter and the answer comes from Wikipedia.
body: The title screen. The blank is a dropdown of categories. Those "What kind of X are you?" quizzes are everywhere. What sandwich are you. What 90s sitcom character are you. They all have the same shape: a fixed set of multiple-choice questions, a mapping from answers to results, and a reveal. The questions are generic personality questions that could map to anything. The category doesn't matter. So I built one where the category is a parameter. You pick a topic from a dropdown, the title fills in ("Countries" becomes "What Country Are You?"), and the result is pulled live from Wikipedia . Where the categories come from The dropdown itself comes from Wikipedia. On each load I pick 5 of 15 broad root categories (Nature, Science, Food and drink, Organisms, Sports, and so on), fetch their subcategories through the MediaWiki API , keep the single-word names between 4 and 14 characters, shuffle, and show 25. If that turns up fewer than 10, a fixed list of 25 fills in instead. So the dropdown is different every time you load the page. The questions and the hash You get 10 questions drawn from a pool of 500, each with four answers. "What is your relationship with your phone at 2% battery?" is one of them, and "My phone is always at 2 percent. We live here now." is one of its answers. When you finish, I take the index of each answer, multiply it by the question's position from 1 to 10, sum the products, and take the total modulo the number of eligible articles in the category. Same answers, same article. The eligible articles are the first 100 pages in the category by sort key, minus anything with "disambiguation", "list of", "index of", "outline of", or "glossary of" in the title, and anything with a slash or a colon. If the category query fails I fall back to a plain search for the category name. A second call fetches the winning article's intro text and a 500 px thumbnail for the reveal. Because the pool is whatever Wikipedia holds today, the result you got last month can be a different article now. The Jeopardy theme There's an mp3 in the repo: the Jeopardy! think music. It starts on your first tap, since browsers won't autoplay audio before a gesture, and its playback rate ramps from 1x at the first question to 3x at the last, in 0.3 second glides so it never jumps. By question 8 it's noticeably frantic. It's the thing people mention when they send the link to someone. The whole app is one 1,391-line HTML file plus the mp3, six commits, and the only thing it talks to is Wikipedia.

title: Dependencies
meta: Races two ways of finding which declared dependencies a build actually needs.
body: Two grids of 32 dependencies. Greedy on the left, binary search on the right, 4 of them required. A project declares 100 dependencies and needs a handful. The rest are left over from deleted features or already pulled in by something else. The only test available is whether the build passes with a given subset, and each test takes time. I wanted to see how the two obvious strategies compare, so I made a page that runs both side by side on the same grid of squares. The setup is \(M\) declared dependencies of which \(N\) are required, and a build oracle that passes exactly when every required one is in the set. That makes the oracle monotone: if a set builds, so does any superset. Version constraints don't exist here. Real resolvers spend their effort on those, and this page has nothing to say about them. Greedy elimination Start with everything included. Remove one dependency and test. If the build passes, leave it out for good. If it fails, put it back. Move to the next. This takes exactly \(M\) tests no matter what \(N\) is. You know how long it'll take before it starts, which is its one virtue. Binary search The second strategy finds the required dependencies one at a time, leftmost first, each with a binary search. Keep a set of the ones found so far. For a range of positions, test the build with everything included except the left half of the range (the found ones always stay in). If it passes, nothing in that half is required and the search moves to the right half. If it fails, something in the left half is required and the search narrows to it. When the range is down to one position, that's a required dependency. Add it to the found set and start over from the leftmost position not yet found. Each round is a binary search over at most \(M\) positions, so about \(\log_2 M\) tests, and there are \(N\) rounds. Roughly \(N \log_2 M\) tests in total. The information-theoretic floor is \(\log_2 \binom{M}{N}\), which is \(\Theta(N \log(M/N))\), so this is close to the best possible when \(N\) is small. At the default settings, 32 dependencies with 4 required, greedy takes 32 tests and binary search about 20. At 256 with 4 required, greedy takes 256 and binary search about 32. When \(N\) approaches \(M\) it goes the other way. Every round still pays a logarithmic search to find the next required dependency, even though nearly all of them are, so the total climbs past \(M\) and greedy wins. Set \(N = M\) on the sliders and watch binary search lose. Watching it Both grids show the same layout. The squares being tested glow, the ones found to be required turn red, the ones eliminated turn grey. A counter under each grid shows tests so far and required dependencies found. The speed slider goes from 50 to 500 ms per test. At the slow end you can follow each decision. At the fast end you can run a dozen configurations in a minute and get a feel for where the crossover is. When both finish, the one with fewer tests is highlighted. The whole thing is one HTML file with no dependencies, which felt appropriate.

title: FrankenPeanuts
meta: Four random Peanuts panels from 1950 to 2000, stitched into a new strip on every reload.
body: A FrankenPeanuts strip. Peanuts ran from October 2, 1950 to February 13, 2000, every strip drawn by Charles Schulz alone. FrankenPeanuts picks four panels at random from the weekday strips and lays them out as a new four-panel comic. Most of them are incoherent. Some of them are accidentally better than they have any right to be. Hovering a panel shows its original date, and the strip is encoded in the URL hash, so a good one can be copied and sent to someone. Cutting the strips up My first version fetched whole strips from peanuts-search.com at page load and split them in the browser with Canvas pixel reads. It needed a CORS proxy, panels took seconds to appear, and some strips never loaded at all. So I moved the cutting to a one-off batch job and committed the results. A 238-line Python script walks every non-Sunday date in the run (the Sunday strips have a different layout) and fetches the strip image. To find the gutters it takes the middle 80 percent of the image height, every second row, and counts how many pixels in each column have a summed RGB under 180. A column where more than 70 percent of sampled pixels are that dark is a gutter line. Runs of gutter columns collapse to their midpoint, anything within 3 percent of the left or right edge is ignored, and the midpoints become the cut positions. A slice narrower than 5 percent of the strip width is dropped, and so is any panel whose width-to-height ratio is outside 0.55 to 1.45, because a very wide or very narrow panel looks wrong in a square grid. The last run covered 15,456 dates. 14,724 of them produced at least one usable panel, 11,963 produced exactly four, and 732 produced none, usually because the scan of a faded or crooked strip found no clean gutter. That's 55,357 JPEGs, about 1.1 GB, committed straight into the repo alongside a manifest.json that maps each date to its panel files. GitHub hasn't complained yet. Running it on Actions Fifty years of strips through one runner would take too long, so the workflow is a 10-job matrix, each job taking a 5-year slice of the archive with 16 fetch threads and a 50 ms pause per request. Each job uploads its partial manifest and its panels as artifacts. A merge job downloads all of them, combines the manifests with a 42-line script, and commits the manifest and images back to the repo. The whole archive takes a few minutes. The script also skips any date already present in its output manifest, so an interrupted local run can be picked up, though on Actions every job starts from nothing. The page itself is one HTML file. It loads the manifest, flattens it into a pool of 55,357 panels, picks four, and shows them in a grid, four across on desktop and two across under 600 px. There is no proxy and nothing to wait for.

title: Haiku
meta: A screensaver that generates a new haiku every ten seconds from a small grammar.
body: A generated haiku. I wanted a screensaver that wrote poetry. Not well, necessarily, but with the right shape and at least a passing resemblance to something a person might say. So this page makes a new haiku every ten seconds, fades it in over a slowly moving background, and never stops. The hard constraint is 5, 7, 5 syllables. Picking random words and hoping they add up almost never works, and when it does the result is word salad. I needed the syllable budget enforced exactly and I needed the three lines to sound like they belonged to the same poem. The grammar Each line has its own handful of templates. The first line is scene-setting, so its templates are noun phrases: a scene_np , or noun, preposition, noun. The second line has to carry a verb, and its four templates all include one. The third line closes, with a close_phrase or an adverb in front of a noun phrase. The nonterminals expand to a sequence of parts of speech, and then I fill that sequence with words whose syllables sum to the line's target. The word bank is a JSON file of 979 words across seven parts of speech, grouped by syllable count. When the filler needs a two-syllable noun it goes straight to that bucket. If a template can't be filled within the budget, I throw it away and try another template rather than forcing a word in. Themes Early versions drew from one big pool. The poems scanned fine and felt random. Snow in line one, the ocean in line two, a forest in line three. So I split the vocabulary into eight themes (winter, spring, summer, autumn, ocean, mountain, night sky, forest), each with its own nouns, verbs, and adjectives. One theme is chosen per poem and every line draws from it. Only when the theme has no word that fits does the filler fall back to general words of three syllables or fewer. Repetition breaks the effect faster than anything else. The same noun in lines one and three, or "the" opening every line, reads as mechanical. I track every word used across the poem and block exact repeats and stem repeats, where one word is a prefix of the other and the shared part is at least three letters. So "drift" in line one blocks "drifting" in line three. Determiners count too, so "the" appears at most once per poem. Only prepositions and conjunctions may repeat. After filling, "a" becomes "an" when the next word starts with a vowel. The auto cycle is ten seconds. A New button skips ahead, and an Auto toggle pauses the cycle. The old poem blurs out and the new one reveals one line at a time, 280 ms apart. Behind it are three blurred colour orbs drifting over a gradient. The whole thing is one HTML file and the JSON word bank, three commits.

title: BrainRotter
meta: Fills a page with grammatical brainrot from a weighted grammar and a 2,277-term lexicon.
body: BrainRotter output. The internet has a dialect. "Skibidi," "rizz," "sigma," and "sus" have their own grammar and usage, opaque to anyone over 25, and I wanted to see what happened when I fed that vocabulary into a proper context-free grammar . Press the button and BrainRotter fills the page with paragraphs of grammatically structured, completely unhinged brainrot . The grammar The engine is a weighted context-free grammar in the style of SCIgen , 910 lines of plain JavaScript. There are 22 weighted sentence types: simple and compound clauses, relative clauses on the subject or the object, nested and compound-complex constructions, conditionals, comparatives, concessives, temporals, three kinds of question, dialogue, meta-commentary, escalation, negation, fake academic citations, enumerations, and callbacks. Simple and compound sentences carry weights of 10 and 9 and enumerations get 2, so the plain structures dominate and the elaborate ones show up often enough to keep the output from looping. The lexicon is 2,277 terms in 13 categories: 419 entities (Skibidi Toilet, Bombardiro Crocodilo, Kai Cenat, Quandale Dingle), 214 transitive and 224 intransitive verbs ("rizzes up," "mogs," "is locked in"), 366 adjectives ("goated," "skibidi-coded," "looksmaxxed"), and then adverbs, prepositional phrases, interjections, and the small categories that glue sentences together. It runs from Among Us through the Italian brainrot era. Morphology The fiddly part was English morphology. Verbs in the lexicon are stored in the third-person present ("rizzes up") because that's how most sentences use them, but a question needs do-support and the bare form. "Skibidi Toilet rizzes up the sigma" has to become "Why did Skibidi Toilet rizz up the sigma?" So deconjugateTV() picks a transitive verb, drops any 's or 'd contraction, finds the first word ending in s, and strips it back with the usual rules: "ies" to "y", "es" to the base unless the stem needs its e, and a plain "s" off unless the word ends in "ss" or "us". Intransitives that start with "is" lose the "is" for the "Is X bussin?" question form. Commas go before a coordinating conjunction between independent clauses and after a leading dependent clause. Those details are the difference between sentences and word salad. A cast and a place Before generating, the engine picks 5 to 8 cast members from the entity pool and 3 recurring locations from the prepositional phrases. Characters are tracked as they're introduced, with a bias toward the cast that eases off as more of them have appeared and a rule against reusing anyone from the last two sentences, so the generator can write callbacks ("Meanwhile, Skibidi Toilet was still...") and consequences that refer to earlier events. Paragraphs come from seven archetypes (opening, narrative, academic, interrogative, dramatic, comparison, freeform), each with its own pool of sentence types, and recent types are remembered so the same construction doesn't land twice in a row. Filling the box The output box has a fixed height and I wanted it exactly full. The generator asks for 30 paragraphs, then adds them one at a time to a hidden div styled to match the box, checking scrollHeight against the box's height after each and stopping before the one that overflows. If there's still room it generates 20 more and keeps going. The text regenerates on resize after a 200 ms pause, and Space or Enter does the same as the button. It's vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with ES modules, loaded straight by the browser. There are PWA icons and a manifest because people were adding it to their home screens, and there are no tests.

title: NYT Crosswords
meta: An ad-free browser player for New York Times crosswords from 1976 to 2017.
body: The puzzle from January 1, 1976. Date picker at the top, grid on the left, across clues on the right. The New York Times crossword is behind a paywall, and the official app is full of ads even when you pay. I like doing old crosswords, the ones from the 70s and 80s where the clues reference things that no longer exist. Someone had already scraped the puzzles from January 1976 through December 2017 into JSON, so I built a page that plays them with no ads and no account. The data The scraped JSON wasn't in the shape react-crossword wants, so I wrote a Python script to convert every puzzle once. The output lives in a second repository as one file per date, and the player fetches the file for whichever date you pick straight from GitHub. There's no server. The coverage gaps are inherited from the source: August 10 to November 5, 1978, and August 30, 2015 to May 1, 2016. The player A date picker at the top takes any date from January 1, 1976 to December 1, 2017, and the 1976 puzzle is baked in so there is something on screen while the first fetch happens. When you finish a word correctly the clue turns green and gets crossed out. There are three buttons, Focus, Fill all answers, and Reset. No timer, no scoring, no streaks. I wanted it to feel like a crossword on paper. I considered building the grid from scratch. react-crossword already handled keyboard navigation, cell highlighting, clue-to-grid sync, and answer checking. Writing all of that from zero would have taken weeks and the result would have been worse. The whole app is 187 lines of React on top of it, plus the date picker. The interesting part was the data conversion, and that part is done.

title: Flow
meta: An RSVP speed reader that starts slow and ramps up, so the opening sentence lands.
body: Flow's text input screen. Rapid Serial Visual Presentation flashes words one at a time at a fixed spot on the screen. The eyes never move, so the saccades that take up most of the time in ordinary reading go away, and 500 to 800 words a minute is comfortable after a few sessions. I tried several RSVP apps and they all had the same problem. They start at the target speed. The first sentence is gone before I've engaged with the text, and the opening is the part everything after it builds on. Flow exists to fix that one thing. The ramp Playback starts at 120 WPM and climbs to the target, 650 by default, over the first 80 words. The speed follows \(t^3\) from 120 to the target, where \(t\) is the fraction of the ramp completed, so the first twenty words barely speed up and the last twenty do most of the climbing. The ramp is capped at 60% of the text so a short passage doesn't spend its whole length accelerating, and floored at ten words. I tried linear first and it felt abrupt. Quadratic was better but I could still feel the moment it kicked in. Cubic was the first curve where I stopped noticing the speed change and just found myself reading faster. By the time the body of the text arrives I'm at full speed and in a rhythm, and the opening, where the author sets the scene, played at a pace I could take in. The pivot letter Each word is split around one letter, which is drawn in amber and pinned to the same horizontal position every time, with a thin vertical guide under it. A three-letter word and a twelve-letter word both put that letter in the same place, so there's nothing to hunt for within a flash. The letter is the one just past the midpoint, index \(\lceil n/2 \rceil\) for an \(n\)-letter word. Other RSVP readers put the anchor about a third of the way in, where eye-tracking studies say the first fixation tends to land. Mine is at the midpoint, and I haven't compared the two. Reading real ebooks I wanted to read my own library, not pasted text, so Flow opens EPUB, MOBI, AZW, AZW3, FB2, PDF, DOCX, RTF, Markdown, HTML, and plain text, all in the browser. EPUB and DOCX are zip archives of XML, which JSZip opens. PDFs go through pdf.js . FB2 is XML. Markdown gets a hand-written CommonMark-to-text converter. The Kindle formats were the work. MOBI and AZW3 are PalmDB containers, and the text records in classic MOBI are compressed with PalmDOC , a small LZ77 variant, so I wrote the decompressor. It's about 30 lines. A byte from 1 to 8 means that many literal bytes follow. 0x09 to 0x7F is a literal. 0x80 to 0xBF starts a two-byte back-reference with an 11-bit distance and a 3-bit length plus three, copying from output already written. 0xC0 to 0xFF is a space followed by the byte with its high bit cleared, a special case for the most common two-character sequence in English prose. For AZW3 the parser scans for the BOUNDARY record that marks the KF8 section and reads the HTML records after it. HUFF/CDIC compressed MOBI files throw an error suggesting a conversion to EPUB, and .kfx is refused outright since it's encrypted. The decoder assumes windows-1252 text and never reads the encoding field in the MOBI header, so a UTF-8 MOBI comes out with mangled accents. I know about it and haven't fixed it. After extraction the text is stripped of HTML tags, Markdown markers, URLs, and email addresses, each token loses the punctuation on both ends, and anything without a letter in it is dropped. Markup showing up as a flashed word is the thing to avoid. Timing The timer is a chained setTimeout with delay 60000 / WPM, rescheduled after each word, inside a hook called useSpeedReader that owns the index, the current WPM, and play, pause, and seek. At 650 WPM a word gets 92 ms. Jitter of 20 to 30 ms shows up as an uneven rhythm, and React re-renders are where it comes from, so the hook keeps the index and the timer handle in refs and a re-render never resets the schedule. The progress bar doubles as a seek control, the WPM field accepts 100 to 1200, and the theme persists in localStorage. It's 1,431 lines of React 18 on Vite including the CSS, most of them the ebook parser, with no tests and no CI.

title: Perfect Hindsight
meta: What a dollar becomes if you hold the best S&P 500 stock every single trading day.
body: Portfolio value on a log scale for one horizon, with the summary table of all 50 horizons below. Buy an index fund, hold it for 30 years, retire. Fine. I wanted the other end of the scale: what if you knew, every morning, which S&P 500 stock would go up the most that day, and put everything in it? One stock per day, long only, no margin. How much money is that? Over 50 years, starting February 13, 1976, a dollar becomes about \(10^{1078}\) dollars. Over one year it's about \(10^{11}\). There are about \(10^{80}\) atoms in the observable universe, so the 50-year number stopped meaning anything around the 8 percent mark. The number is useless as a target. It's useful as a ceiling: no long-only daily strategy on this universe can beat it, and the gap between it and an index fund is a measure of how much return is locked behind information nobody has. The arithmetic Let \( S_t \) be the stocks in the index on day \( t \) and \( r_{i,t} \) the daily return of stock \( i \). Holding the best one each day gives \[ V_T \;=\; V_0 \prod_{t=1}^{T} \bigl(1 + \max_{i \in S_t}\, r_{i,t}\bigr) \] and the annualized rate solves \( V_T = V_0\,(1+r_a)^{T/252} \), so \( r_a = (V_T/V_0)^{252/T} - 1 \). With no transaction cost every day is independent, so the greedy choice is the optimum and there's nothing cleverer to do. I did think about adding a switching cost, which would turn it into a real dynamic program over what you held yesterday, but I haven't built it and the tool has no cost parameter. The rule I actually computed is: all in on the top stock, or cash if every stock fell that day. Cash never happened. With at least 91 stocks in the universe there was always something up, so all 12,605 trading days are a buy, a hold, or a switch, and 12,122 of them are switches. Because the numbers span a thousand orders of magnitude I store and sum \( \log_{10}(1 + r) \) per day rather than multiplying, which is also why the chart is on a log scale. A straight line on it is a constant compounding rate. What the data actually is The numbers were computed offline and the page loads a 1.7 MB precomputed JSON. I haven't published the generator, and the repo doesn't name the price source, so take everything below as a description of that file rather than something you can rerun. Index membership comes from 389 constituent changes scraped from Wikipedia, the earliest dated July 1976, giving 843 tickers over the period, 661 of which had price data. That's what the footer's "survivorship bias mitigated" flag means, and it overstates things. In 1976 the universe has 91 stocks against a 500-stock index. It reaches 182 in 1980, 308 on average over the full run, and only crosses 500 in 2025. The stocks missing from the early years are mostly ones that were delisted or acquired before whichever data vendor started covering them, which is survivorship bias by another route. The recent decade is close to complete. The 1970s and 80s are not. There's at least one bad print. The largest single-day return in the file is TIE (Titanium Metals) on April 3, 2012, at 7,213 times, or +721,300 percent. That's a data error, and on its own it contributes 3.9 of the 1,078 orders of magnitude. I've left it in because I can't rerun the generator, and because it makes the point that the headline number is a ceiling on the data, not on the market. The most-held names are not the ones I expected. Cooper Industries (CBE) and Nabors Industries (NBR) each won about 430 days over 50 years, then El Paso (EP), Rockwell Collins (COL), Western Digital (WDC), Goodrich (GR), Micron (MU), and AMD. Volatile stocks dominate because a stock that swings 10 percent in a day is the best performer on a lot of its up days, and the winner-take-all rule never cares about the down days. The page shows one horizon at a time, from 1 to 50 years back from February 13, 2026, with the final value, return multiple, annualized rate, trade count, and a bar chart of which stocks were held most. Hovering the line shows that day's stock and its return. The table below lists all 50 horizons and clicking a row switches the chart.

title: Wikipedia Unscrambler
meta: A word game that scrambles a passage from one of yesterday's most-read Wikipedia articles
body: A 120-word passage with every word scrambled, and the title guess box below it. The typoglycemia meme says you can read jumbled text as long as the first and last letters stay put. That's an overstatement, but context clearly does a lot of the work when you read, and I wanted a game that measured how much. So this scrambles every letter of every word, first and last included, and gives you nothing but the words around it. The game fetches a real article, cuts out four sentences, and shuffles each word in place with punctuation left where it was. You type your guess for each word into its slot and it locks green when you're right. Separately, you can guess the article title at any point. The two tasks feed each other: a few unscrambled words tell you the topic, and the topic tells you what the remaining words could be. Three hints are available for the title, in order the character count, the first letter, and the first word. Yesterday's top 500 as a difficulty dial Not all articles are equally guessable. The United States has vocabulary anyone knows. A particular species of moth does not. The one idea in this project is to use Wikimedia's pageview API as the difficulty signal: I pull yesterday's 500 most-viewed articles on English Wikipedia, drop the Main Page and anything with a namespace prefix, and slice by rank. Easy is the top 50, medium is 50 to 200, hard is 200 to 500. Easy comes out as countries, celebrities, and whatever was in the news. Hard is articles I've never opened. Because the ranking is a day old, the puzzles rotate on their own. Someone who trends on a Tuesday is an easy puzzle on Wednesday and gone by Thursday. I never have to curate a list. A few small choices matter more than they look. If the article has more than ten sentences I skip the first three to six before taking my four, because the lede usually names the subject outright. Extracts under 200 characters get thrown away and another article drawn. All three difficulties are fetched at once and keep their own state, so switching from easy to hard doesn't lose the easy puzzle. The whole thing is one 610-line HTML file with two commits. The pageview and extract APIs both allow cross-origin requests, so there's nothing for a server to do.

title: Anagram Solver
meta: Every way to rearrange a phrase into real words, ranked so the good ones come first.
body: The Anagram Solver. Most anagram sites return one result, maybe two. I wanted all of them for a phrase, with the good ones at the top, and that's a different problem from finding one. The solver takes a phrase, reduces it to a letter count, rebuilds every combination of dictionary words that uses those letters exactly, and ranks them. Letter counts Every word is a 26-byte array, one count per letter. The 20,000-word dictionary is embedded in the WebAssembly binary with include_str! and converted at startup, and the input phrase gets the same treatment. Checking whether a word fits the remaining letters is 26 comparisons and taking it out is 26 subtractions, which is what keeps the inner loop cheap when the search gets deep. Before searching I filter the dictionary to words that fit inside the phrase at all and sort them longest first, so the branches with long words get explored first. The search It's a depth-first search. At each level I walk the candidate list from a start index, take any word that fits, subtract its letters, and recurse with the start index set to that word's position, so the same set of words can't come out in two orders. Without that, "star wars" and "wars star" would both appear. On top of that there's a signature check I'm less happy with. Each finished result records the sorted set of its words of four or more letters, and any branch that would reproduce a set already seen is pruned. It kills the flood of results that differ only in how the leftover short words are arranged, which is what I wanted, but it also drops legitimate anagrams that happen to share their long words with an earlier one. The search also stops at 50,000 raw results, and once it has 5,000 it stops descending into words shorter than a depth-dependent minimum unless five or fewer letters remain. Those cutoffs are why "William Shakespeare" comes back at all. Ranking A phrase that long produces thousands of results and most are garbage, strings of two-letter words that use the right letters and interest no one. The score is 100 points per letter of average word length, minus 1,000 per word, minus 5 per unit of total deviation from the average length. A two-word anagram with balanced lengths lands far above a seven-word one made of "is" and "at" and "me". Results come back sorted by that score, deduplicated, and capped at 10,000. In the browser It's 337 lines of Rust compiled with wasm-pack , with no server involved. The whole search runs on the main thread behind a spinner, so a long phrase freezes the page while it thinks. A worker would fix that and I haven't bothered. The dictionary is also re-parsed from the embedded text on every call, which is wasted work. There are no tests.

title: Lasers
meta: Place and rotate mirrors to bounce a laser around obstacles and into a target
body: A fresh level. The beam stops at the circle that always sits on the straight line to the target. A laser fires from the left edge of an 800 by 600 board and a target sits on the right edge. Circles in between block the straight shot, and you place mirrors to bounce the beam around them. Fewer mirrors is a better score. I've seen this as a physical board game in toy shops. On a screen it gets unlimited levels for free. Tracing the beam The beam is a ray and each mirror is a 60-pixel segment. For every mirror I solve the ray-segment intersection as a 2x2 linear system and keep the hit only if the ray parameter is positive and the segment parameter is between 0 and 1. For every circle, substituting the ray into \(|\mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}|^2 = R^2\) gives a quadratic in \(t\), and a non-negative discriminant is a hit. The nearest hit wins. An obstacle or the board edge ends the beam. The target ends it with a win. A mirror with unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) reflects it, \[\mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}})\,\hat{\mathbf{n}},\] and the trace carries on, up to 50 bounces so two facing mirrors can't hang the page. Mirrors rotate continuously rather than snapping to 45 degrees, and the whole path is retraced every frame while one is still being turned, so the beam sweeps across the board until it lands. Levels Each level is random rather than seeded. The first obstacle always goes on the straight line between laser and target, somewhere between 30 and 70 percent of the way across, offset by less than its own radius so the direct shot is blocked. Then 5 plus twice the level number more circles, 18 to 35 pixels in radius, land at random with at least 50 pixels of clearance around the laser and the target and 10 between each other. A circle that can't find a spot in 100 tries is dropped. The layout is base64-encoded into a game parameter in the URL, so a link to the page is a link to that exact puzzle and someone else can try to beat your mirror count on it. The whole game is one HTML file drawing to a canvas . The beam is the only bright thing on a dark board, and the target turns green when it's hit. There are no score popups and no particles.

title: Papermaker
meta: SCIgen's fake computer science papers, generated in the browser and typeset to PDF.
body: The Papermaker interface. In 2005 three MIT grad students, Jeremy Stribling, Max Krohn, and Dan Aguayo, built SCIgen , which generates fake computer science papers from a context-free grammar . They submitted one to the World Multiconference on Systemics, Cybernetics and Informatics and it was accepted. It was called " Rooter: A Methodology for the Typical Unification of Access Points and Redundancy " and it meant nothing at all. Papermaker is SCIgen in the browser. One click produces a typeset two-column PDF with a title, abstract, introduction, related work, a methodology, results with figures, a conclusion, and references. The papers have the right shape and the right density of jargon and say nothing. Skimmed the way a tired reviewer skims, they pass. The grammar SCIgen's grammar is a 3,777-line text file of production rules, each a symbol followed by one expansion, with alternatives listed as repeated rules and picked at random. It knows that a results section refers to figures, that figures have axes and legends, and that related work cites authors and venues. Two rule suffixes give it a little memory. A counter rule hands out the next integer each time it fires, and a companion rule draws a random integer below the current count, which is how a \ref ends up pointing at a figure that exists. Perl to Rust to the browser The original is Perl and writes LaTeX to disk. I rewrote the expansion engine in Rust and compiled it to WebAssembly with wasm-pack . It's 364 lines: a hash map of rules, a seeded SmallRng so a seed reproduces a paper, the counters, and a recursive expand. The grammar file and the graph grammar are fetched at runtime inside a Web Worker, and the worker fixes capitalization after sentence boundaries and in titles once the expansion is done. Figures and the compile The figures are my favorite part of the output. SCIgen's grammar emits gnuplot commands and graphviz for them, which was fine on a Unix box in 2005 and is useless in a browser, so a second worker rewrites them. It parses the gnuplot commands into pgfplots charts of throughput against input size with a few fictional series, seeded from the command text so the same paper gets the same chart, and turns the graphviz figures into TikZ flowcharts of boxes labeled with the paper's own component names. The bibliography gets the same treatment. BibTeX can't run, so the worker generates the entries and inlines a thebibliography environment. The data is random and the presentation is right, and a figure looked at on its own passes for an experimental result. Then the LaTeX goes to latex.ytotech.com, a free compilation service with CORS enabled, and a PDF comes back. That service is the one piece of the project I don't run. If it goes away, Papermaker stops producing PDFs until I find another one or compile in the browser the way eigencircuits does. There are no tests and the build is a shell script.

title: The Count of Monte Carlo
meta: Random characters settle into the text of Dumas one letter at a time.
body: The first of 5,805 passages, complete after 440 frames. The page loads The Count of Monte Cristo from a bundled copy of the Project Gutenberg text, starting at "On the 24th of February", and cuts it into passages of about 100 words, breaking at a full stop where it can. Each passage starts as noise. Every letter, digit, and punctuation mark is replaced with a random character from a pool of 91. Spaces and line breaks stay where they are, so the paragraph keeps its shape while the words are gibberish. Then, on every animation frame, each wrong character gets a 3% chance to snap to its correct value. That's the whole mechanism. With \(n\) wrong characters left, the expected number still wrong after \(t\) more frames is \(n(0.97)^t\). From 100 wrong characters to 1 takes about \(\ln(0.01)/\ln(0.97) \approx 151\) frames, two and a half seconds at 60 fps. The last character on its own waits 33 frames on average, and the very end of every passage is a finished paragraph with one letter still flickering. That tail is the maximum of many independent waits, and it's the part I find most watchable. The code is messier than that. The loop scans the passage in reading order and stops after five changes per frame, and the first couple of those are usually spent re-randomising a wrong character so the noise keeps moving. So a fresh passage resolves from the front in a wave, and the pure 3% behaviour only takes over once about a hundred characters remain. There's a comment in the code about randomising the scan order to avoid exactly this bias. The array under it is sequential. I've left it, because the wave looks fine. Words surface before their sentences do. A character's name appears, then the verb, then the rest of the line around them. The page updates the DOM every other frame, keeps a count of frames and a percentage of correct characters, and has previous, next, and skip buttons for moving through the passages. It's one HTML file and the text file, set in Georgia on a cream panel over dark brown.

title: Creature Garden
meta: A single-file ecosystem sandbox where procedural creatures eat, breed, and starve on a canvas.
body: Creature Garden mid-run, with the stats bar at the top. I wanted to build a petri dish you could watch. Drop some creatures into a space with limited food and see what happens. They eat, they grow, they reproduce, they die. The population booms, overshoots, crashes, and recovers, in the way populations do when they share a resource that comes back at a fixed rate. You can intervene by dropping food wherever you click, or you can leave it alone and watch. None of that is modelled. There are no equations for population in the code, no Lotka-Volterra, no logistic curve. The oscillation comes out of a handful of per-creature rules and a constant food spawn rate, and it has the same shape those models describe, which is the fun of it. The creatures Each creature gets random traits: a body colour from anywhere on the hue wheel, a diameter between 6 and 25 pixels, and six to nine tentacles. The tentacles animate with a sine undulation, so each creature has its own swimming motion. Two white eyes with black pupils sit on the body. They land somewhere between a cartoon octopus and something from a plankton net. Eating makes a creature grow, and the per-frame energy cost grows with the square of the radius, so a creature twice as wide burns four times as fast. Past some size, intake can't keep up and it starves. I didn't program a size cap. The square law is the cap. What they do Creatures have three drives. They steer toward nearby food. They push away from each other at close range. They flee the cursor inside a 100-pixel radius. Each frame the drives sum into an acceleration, and velocity carries over with a drag factor below 1 so nothing teleports. They drift, turn, speed up toward food, and scatter when the cursor gets close. Food spawns at random positions at a constant rate and disappears after 300 frames if nobody reaches it. That constant rate is the whole carrying capacity. Too many creatures and they compete for what's there. Too few and food sits uneaten until it vanishes. Clicking adds food at the cursor, which raises the ceiling for as long as you keep clicking. Birth and death Every frame, every living creature has a 1 percent chance of spawning a new one nearby. Offspring get fresh random traits rather than a copy of the parent, so the garden stays visually varied. With that rate, a creature that lives 200 frames has an 87 percent chance of reproducing at least once, and one that dies at 50 frames has 39 percent. Nothing selects on traits. Creatures that happen to be near food live longer and get more rolls of the dice, which is as close to natural selection as this gets. Death has two clocks. A hunger counter climbs every frame and resets on eating, and when it crosses a threshold the creature dies. A lifespan counter runs alongside it, and a well-fed creature still dies when that runs out. Either one ends it. The stats bar shows the current living count, the food count, and a score. The whole thing is one HTML file with a Canvas 2D render loop. The background is a dark blue-green gradient, the creatures are bright, and the cursor drags a faint blue glow so you can tell where the thing they're fleeing from is.

title: Random Game
meta: Tells you what to guess next in a closest-number-wins game with other players.
body: Three inputs for the range and the latest guess, and the recommended next guess below. There's an icebreaker where someone picks a number in a range, say 1 to 100, everyone guesses, and the closest wins. Alone it's binary search . With other people guessing too, the midpoint of the whole range stops being the right move. You want the midpoint of the largest stretch nobody has claimed yet, because that's where you have the best chance of being closest. I built this for a recurring office game where the prize was picking the lunch restaurant. I kept losing because I was guessing "intuitively" and competing with everyone else's intuition for the same part of the number line. Most people guess round numbers. They cluster around multiples of 10 and especially around 50, and it's common to see three people guess in the 40 to 60 range while the ends of the range sit empty. After switching to this I won noticeably more often. What it does You enter the minimum, the maximum, and each guess as it's made. It sorts the bounds and the guesses, finds the widest gap between neighbours, and tells you the midpoint of that gap. If the number is uniform on the range, the chance it falls in a gap is proportional to the gap's width, so the widest gap is the best bet and bisecting it is the greedy move. With the range 1 to 100 and a guess of 30, the gaps are 1 to 30 and 30 to 100, so it says 65. If someone then guesses 80, the widest gap is 30 to 80 and it says 55. The whole thing is one HTML page with about 20 lines of JavaScript and no dependencies. It assumes the number is uniform, which the person picking it usually isn't, and it doesn't try to model that.

title: License Plate Game
meta: Type the three letters from a plate and get the shortest words that contain them in order.
body: Three letters typed in, and the ten shortest words that contain them in order. There's a road trip game where you take the three letters on a license plate and try to think of a word that contains them in that order, not necessarily adjacent. You see BRN and someone shouts BURNING. You see PLT and there's PLATFORM. The difficulty varies wildly. Some combinations have dozens of common answers and others seem impossible until someone finds the one obscure word that works. I built this to settle arguments. You type three letters and it shows the shortest words that contain them as a subsequence . It loads a word list on startup and checks every word on each keystroke, walking each word once looking for the three letters in order. It's fast enough that there's no index or precomputation. Results are sorted shortest first and capped at ten, because in the car a short word is the impressive answer. Nobody is impressed by a 14-letter word; three letters are bound to turn up somewhere in something that long. A four-letter word containing XPL wins the round. The whole thing is one HTML page and one word list, and it's laid out for a phone in the passenger seat.
